task_row_model.query: A 45-year-old patient presents with acute unilateral facial droop involving the entire right side of the face but no limb weakness. How can I distinguish Bell's palsy from a cortical stroke at the bedside, and what initial management should I start?

documents.content: Bell's palsy is an acute peripheral facial nerve (VII) palsy often presenting with rapid onset unilateral facial paralysis affecting both the forehead and lower face. Viral reactivation, particularly HSV, is frequently implicated. First-line treatment is a short course of oral corticosteroid initiated within 72 hours of symptom onset to improve recovery. Antiviral therapy such as acyclovir can be considered in severe cases or when herpes is suspected. Eye protection with lubricating drops and eyelid taping at night is essential to prevent corneal damage. Most patients begin to recover within weeks, with many near-complete recoveries by three months.

Trigeminal neuralgia causes sudden, severe, electric shock–like facial pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (V). Attacks are brief, triggered by light touch, chewing, or brushing teeth, and patients are typically asymptomatic between episodes. There is usually no motor deficit of facial expression muscles. Diagnosis is clinical but can be supported by MRI to exclude secondary causes. First-line pharmacologic treatment is carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine. Surgical options are considered for refractory cases. Sensory symptoms and sharp paroxysmal pain distinguish this disorder from motor neuropathies of the facial nerve.

Distinguish peripheral (Bell's) facial palsy from central (cortical) stroke by the pattern of weakness: peripheral VII palsy affects both the upper and lower face, producing inability to raise the eyebrow or close the eye on the affected side. A central lesion typically spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation and causes weakness of the contralateral lower face only. At bedside, examine forehead movement, check for limb weakness, speech disturbance, gaze palsies, sensory deficits, and cerebellar signs. If isolated full-face paralysis with forehead involvement and no other deficits, start oral corticosteroids within 72 hours, provide eye protection, consider antiviral therapy if severe, and arrange outpatient follow-up. Obtain urgent imaging if any focal deficits or stroke suspicion persists.

Ischemic cortical strokes affecting the motor cortex can produce contralateral lower facial weakness while sparing the forehead due to bilateral cortical contribution to upper facial muscles. Acute stroke often presents with additional findings such as limb weakness, sensory loss, dysarthria, visual field defects, or gaze deviation. Use the FAST mnemonic (Face, Arms, Speech, Time) to screen and proceed to urgent non-contrast CT to exclude hemorrhage if thrombolysis is being considered. Management focuses on reperfusion therapies within the appropriate time window, antiplatelet therapy, and secondary prevention of vascular risk factors after the acute phase.

Facial cellulitis is a bacterial skin and soft tissue infection characterized by localized erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness. It may be accompanied by fever and regional lymphadenopathy. Unlike cranial neuropathies, cellulitis produces visible skin changes and often a clear portal of entry such as trauma or insect bite. Treatment requires appropriate systemic antibiotics targeting common organisms like Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci, and severe cases may need IV therapy and surgical evaluation. Neurologic motor deficits are not typical of uncomplicated cellulitis.
